Does long-term 3PL storage flip a fulfillment quote?

A rate card prices every pallet at the fresh-storage line. After leftover sits past 30–90 days, most 3PLs move those pallets onto a higher long-term rate. Months to eat a liquidation recovery is leftover recovery divided by leftover times the long-term rate.

Does the total include returns and restocking, not just outbound fees?

pallet-vs-carton-inbound.html.text:
← 3PL inbound method calculator

Why pallet inbound usually beats carton inbound on the same 3PL quote

Brands search for “3PL inbound fee” or “pallet inbound vs carton inbound” after a warehouse sends a rate card with three receiving lines. The card looks complete. The decision is still missing: at your units per pallet and units per carton, which line is the cheap one?

The arithmetic is the fee divided by the units in the container. A $10 pallet that holds 60 units is $0.17 per unit. A $1.50 carton that holds 6 units is $0.25 per unit. Loose / floor-unload receiving at $0.40 per unit is $0.40. On 480 inbound units that is $80 versus $120 versus $192 — a $112 monthly gap — before storage, pick, or shipping move at all.

Warehouses like loose receiving because it is easy to quote and hard to compare. You can often ship the same goods palletized, or ask the 3PL to receive against the pallet line, and keep the rest of the quote. A monthly minimum can still swallow the difference; the calculator shows that case instead of pretending the receiving line disappeared.

This is a different question from leftover pallets already on the floor, from restocking a return, and from paying the 3PL to kit. Those extras live on long-term storage, restock vs keep, and kitting.

Rates change by building, freight class, and appointment type. This page does not publish anyone’s live schedule. Open the inbound method calculator, type the three lines from your rate card, and see which method wins at your volume.

The result is arithmetic, not advice. It does not say you should palletize, change carriers, or sign a warehouse.

Common questions

Is pallet inbound cheaper than carton inbound at a 3PL?

Usually, because the fee is divided by the units in the container. A $10 pallet that holds 60 units is $0.17 per unit. A $1.50 carton that holds 6 units is $0.25 per unit. Loose receiving at $0.40 per unit is $0.40. On 480 inbound units that is $80 versus $120 versus $192.

Can a monthly minimum hide the inbound difference?

Yes. When the rest of the quote already sits under a monthly minimum, a cheaper receiving line does not change the normalized total. The inbound calculator shows that case instead of pretending the receiving line disappeared.

Common questions

Should I pay a 3PL to kit or skip the bundle?

The signed pick-and-pack line prices the first unit. Ops then bills assembly, extra component picks, and extra receiving. Pre-kitting before inbound keeps those extra 3PL lines at zero and pays only your labor. Skipping the kit keeps the hero SKU and forgoes the AOV lift. On a typical $6 lift / $2.80 extra COGS / $3.50 kit fee / $1 extra picks / $0.36 extra receiving bundle, 3PL assembly loses $1.66 per kit versus skipping it, while pre-kitting keeps $2.30.

When does paying the 3PL to assemble beat skipping the kit?

Subtract extra COGS, extra picks, and extra receiving from the AOV lift. That leftover is the highest kit fee that still beats skip. At the default $6 lift, $2.80 extra COGS, $1 extra picks, and $0.36 extra receiving, 3PL assembly first beats skip at a $1.84 kit fee or a $7.66 AOV lift.

Common questions

Should I restock a 3PL return or let the customer keep it?

The sale is already refunded. Restock pays the prepaid label, inbound return handling, inspect/putaway, and storage until it sells again, then writes off the unsellable fraction. Destroy pays the label, inbound, and a dispose fee, then writes off the full unit cost. Customer-keeps skips the label and the 3PL return lines and writes off the unit. On a cheap SKU with an expensive label, letting them keep it is usually cheaper. Restock wins once unit cost covers those extra 3PL fees at your restockable rate.

When does restocking beat letting the customer keep a return?

Divide the extra 3PL path (label + inbound + restock + storage + leftover destroy) by the restockable rate. That is the unit-cost threshold. At the default $8 label, $3.50 inbound, $4 restock, $0.40 storage, $1.50 leftover destroy, and 70% restockable, restock first beats customer-keeps at $23.36 cost of goods.

vs-extensiv.html.text:
← 3PL Quote Normalizer

3PL Quote Normalizer vs. Extensiv

Two different shapes: Extensiv is warehouse and order management software you operate through every day. This page is a free worksheet for one narrower moment — deciding whether the 3PL quote in front of you is actually cheaper than doing it in-house — before any warehouse system is involved.

What each tool is for

Extensiv (formerly 3PL Central) is warehouse and order management software, publicly documented as a cloud-based platform used by third-party logistics providers, and by brands running their own warehouses, to manage inventory, orders, billing, and fulfillment operations across one or more facilities. It is an account-based platform: an operator signs up and runs day-to-day warehouse and order operations through it as an ongoing subscription, not a one-off calculator. Extensiv's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — warehouse and order management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Extensiv appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Extensiv does. It does not manage inventory, route an order to a pick path, or connect to a warehouse or a sales channel. It takes the rate-card lines already sitting in a 3PL quote — receiving, storage, pick and pack, packaging, shipping, returns and return handling, restocking, fixed fees, and any monthly minimum — and turns them into a comparable monthly total, a true cost per order, and the order volume where that quote's minimum charge or per-order pricing stops beating an in-house estimate you supply. It also has dedicated pages for the fine print a flat "chemical cost"-style percentage usually misses: leftover pallets aging into long-term storage, restocking a return versus letting the customer keep it, paying the 3PL to kit versus skipping the bundle, and which inbound method (pallet, carton, or loose) is actually cheaper at your volume. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a 3PL, or a brand's own warehouse, and need to manage inventory, orders, billing, and fulfillment day to day.Extensiv, or a comparable WMS — running a warehouse is not something this calculator does.
Is the 3PL quote I just received actually cheaper than doing it in-house, once minimums and returns are counted?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
At what order volume does a 3PL's minimum charge stop being the real price driver?This calculator's volume sensitivity page.
Does a leftover pallet aging into long-term storage change a quote that looked cheap on the fresh-storage line?This calculator's long-term storage page.
I need one shared system so my whole team is managing inventory and orders the same way, across facilities.Extensiv, or a comparable WMS.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Extensiv is used through a subscription account.

Most growing brands get different value from each, often at different stages: this calculator to decide whether a 3PL quote is worth signing and to negotiate it with an itemized brief, and Extensiv or a comparable WMS once there is a warehouse — a 3PL's or the brand's own — that needs to be run day to day as an ongoing account. This page's own figures are a cost model built from numbers you supply, not a live quote, a contract, or a fulfillment-operations audit.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, your quote is saved to this browser's local storage only, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Extensiv?

They answer different questions, and a growing brand may end up using both at different stages. Extensiv is warehouse and order management software: an account-based platform that a 3PL, or a brand running its own warehouse, operates through every day to manage inventory, orders, and fulfillment across one or more facilities, sold as an ongoing subscription. This calculator does one narrower thing before any of that: it takes the rate-card lines from a 3PL quote you already have in hand — receiving, storage, pick and pack, packaging, shipping, returns, fixed fees, and any monthly minimum — and turns them into a comparable monthly total, a true cost per order, and the order volume where that quote stops being cheaper than doing it in-house. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. Someone choosing or negotiating a 3PL quote is in the right place here; a 3PL or brand that already has a warehouse to run day to day needs Extensiv or a comparable WMS, not this page.

Does this calculator replace a warehouse management system?

No. It does not track inventory, route orders, manage pick paths, or connect to a warehouse, a 3PL's systems, or a sales channel. It takes numbers you already have — the lines on a rate card and your own in-house cost per order — and computes a monthly total, a cost per order, and a break-even volume from them. 3PL Quote Normalizer vs. normalizing the quote yourself in a spreadsheet

The arithmetic is the same either way: a rate card's receiving, storage, pick and pack, packaging, shipping, returns, and fixed-fee lines add up to a monthly total, a cost per order, and a break-even volume. The difference is whether the sheet already prompts you to check the monthly minimum, aged storage, kitting, and return disposition, or whether you have to remember all four yourself while comparing three quotes under a deadline.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can produce exactly the same normalized monthly total as this calculator — summing rate-card lines and comparing the result to an in-house estimate is not exotic math. What a blank spreadsheet does not give you is a structure that already checks whether the monthly minimum, rather than the per-order lines you priced, is the number actually setting the bill, or a place that re-runs the same quote through aged long-term storage, kitting, and return-disposition comparisons without you having to build each one from scratch.

This calculator is that structure already built. Type the rate-card lines once and it computes the monthly total, true cost per order, and break-even order volume, then reuses the same figures in dedicated sub-calculators for the fine print a flat total usually hides: aged long-term storage, kitting, and return disposition. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is the quote I just received actually cheaper than doing it in-house?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Is the monthly minimum, not my per-order lines, what's really setting the bill?This calculator's “Minimum charge applied?” row, checked automatically on every quote you type.
Does a leftover pallet aging into long-term storage change a quote that looked cheap on the fresh-storage line?This calculator's long-term storage comparison, reusing the same quote.
My rate card has a shape this calculator doesn't model (per-SKU tiers, a currency other than dollars).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any structure you can describe.
Is my rate-card data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, your quote is saved to this browser's local storage only, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this calculator?

A correctly built one is — turning a rate card into a monthly total, a cost per order, and a break-even volume is ordinary arithmetic. The risk is not the math, it is remembering every line that can move the real number: whether the monthly minimum, not the per-order lines, is actually setting the bill; whether a leftover pallet has aged into long-term storage at a different rate than the fresh-storage line quoted; and how kitting fees and return disposition change the total once they apply. A spreadsheet built under deadline, comparing three quotes at once, is exactly where one of those gets left out.

When is a spreadsheet actually the better choice?

When your rate card has a shape this calculator does not model — a per-SKU tiered rate, a currency other than dollars, or a fee structure that does not map to receiving, storage, pick and pack, packaging, shipping, returns, restocking, fixed fees, and a monthly minimum. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any structure you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields, and the sub-calculators, for the common case: comparing a 3PL's rate card against doing it in-house.

What does a blank spreadsheet not remind you to do that this calculator does?

Check whether the monthly minimum, not the per-order lines you priced, is what actually sets the bill below a certain volume — and run the same rate card through the dedicated aged-storage, kitting, and return-disposition comparisons, each of which uses the exact totals from the quote you already typed. A spreadsheet built from scratch has no built-in prompt for any of the three; this calculator raises each one as its own numbered result rather than leaving it for you to remember to model.

Does this replace a signed contract or a fulfillment operations audit?

No, and neither does a spreadsheet. Both stop at estimating a comparable monthly total and cost per order from the rate-card figures you supply. Neither one audits the 3PL's actual operations, verifies the contract language, or accounts for a fee not listed on the card you were quoted. That review still belongs to you before you sign anything.

3PL Quote Normalizer vs. ShipBob

ShipBob is one specific 3PL you would sign a fulfillment contract with. This page is a free worksheet for a different moment — you already have a quote in hand, from ShipBob or anyone else, and want to know whether it actually beats doing it in-house.

What each one is for

ShipBob is publicly documented as a third-party logistics provider: a network of fulfillment centers that receives, stores, and ships inventory on a brand's behalf under a signed contract, priced per account after you submit your volume, SKU count, and shipping profile. It is one option among many 3PLs a brand might quote, and its own pricing is not published as a flat rate card -- like most 3PLs, it is quoted per account, so no dollar figure for ShipBob is invented here.

This calculator does not compete with ShipBob for your fulfillment business, and it cannot get you a ShipBob quote. It does the opposite job: once you have a quote -- from ShipBob, from a competing 3PL, or from several you are weighing against each other -- you type its rate-card lines in here: receiving, storage, pick and pack, packaging, shipping, returns and return handling, restocking, fixed fees, and any monthly minimum. The calculator turns those into a comparable monthly total, a true cost per order, and the order volume where that quote's minimum charge or per-order pricing stops beating an in-house estimate you supply. Its dedicated pages cover the fine print a single blended rate usually hides: leftover pallets aging into long-term storage, restocking a return versus letting the customer keep it, paying to kit versus skipping the bundle, and which inbound method is cheaper at your volume -- questions that apply the same way whichever 3PL sent the quote. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have not requested a quote yet and want to know what ShipBob would charge.ShipBob directly — this calculator has no connection to their pricing and cannot quote you.
I have a quote from ShipBob (or another 3PL) and want to know if it beats doing it in-house.This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
I have quotes from two or more 3PLs, ShipBob included, and want to compare them side by side.This calculator's multi-quote comparison page.
At what order volume does a 3PL's minimum charge stop being the real price driver?This calculator's volume sensitivity page.
Do I need to create an account or sign a contract to check the arithmetic on a quote?This calculator: no. ShipBob and other 3PLs require a signed contract to actually fulfill orders.

A brand evaluating fulfillment options typically uses both, in sequence: ShipBob (and usually a few competing 3PLs) to get quotes, then this calculator to normalize each quote into the same comparable numbers before signing anything. This page's own figures are a cost model built from numbers you supply, not a live quote from ShipBob or verification of any contract.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, your quote is saved to this browser's local storage only, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ShipBob's own quote?

They are not substitutes for each other. ShipBob is a third-party logistics network: a company you would sign a fulfillment contract with, publicly documented as providing warehousing, pick and pack, and shipping across a network of fulfillment centers, priced by requesting a custom quote for your volume and SKUs. This calculator does not provide a quote from ShipBob or any 3PL. It takes a rate-card quote you already have in hand -- from ShipBob, from a competing 3PL, or from several you are comparing -- and turns it into a comparable monthly total, a true cost per order, and the order volume where that quote stops being cheaper than doing it in-house. Someone who already has a ShipBob quote, or one from any other 3PL, and wants to check it against in-house costs or against a competing bid is in the right place here; someone who does not yet have a quote needs to request one from ShipBob or another 3PL first.

Does this calculator get pricing from ShipBob?

No. It has no connection to ShipBob, requests no data from them, and does not know ShipBob's rates. ShipBob, like most 3PLs, quotes custom rates per account rather than publishing a price list, so this page states no dollar figure for ShipBob. You type in the rate-card lines from a quote you already received -- receiving, storage, pick and pack, packaging, shipping, returns, fixed fees, and any monthly minimum -- from ShipBob or any other 3PL, and the calculator does the arithmetic.
